reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes free branded gift cards or codes through a linked reward flow that requires viewers to complete offers or points requirements. The flow also requests an email address, physical address, and date of birth in connection with claims such as a $250 Walmart gift card, although the available video evidence does not establish whether the codes are valid or whether any reward is delivered.

opening.argument: Judge the recording for what it establishes, not for what an external page might ultimately deliver. The description invokes fair use for purposes including teaching and research, while the footage shows a gift-card interface and its conditions, including purchase requirements. That disclaimer is about copyright, not a guarantee that the offer is safe. But the presentation does disclose a condition rather than showing an unconditional handout, and the sampled frames do not establish that anyone received a valid code or suffered a loss. The narrower reading is a screen-recorded examination of an offer whose outcome remains unverified.

citations.quote: for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies a reward flow, sponsor offers, and requests for personal details, but those observations alone do not establish that the creator obtained the information or that the offer failed. The page visibly conditions the Walmart reward on purchase requirements; treating that qualification as an unconditional promise overlooks what the viewer can see.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The fair-use paragraph concerns copyrighted material, not the reliability of gift-card claims or the risks of submitting information. The title advertises free branded cards and codes, and the description directs viewers to a pinned-comment link. The filmed flow then places purported code access behind sponsor offers. A completed loss is not needed to recognize that promotional pattern.

opening.argument: This can be read as a walkthrough of what a gift-card site displays, not proof that the creator can supply working cards. The recording moves from a selection of brands to a Mastercard generator screen, then shows a separate reward questionnaire and an offer-lock screen. Those changing screens are the substance of the video; the supplied speech transcript contains no intelligible pitch explaining that viewers will receive a valid card. Showing an interface, including its barriers, is not the same as verifying its claims or personally issuing its rewards.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's frames show the site's claims and form fields, but they cannot by themselves distinguish endorsement from a recording of those screens. The transcript supplies no coherent spoken assurance that the code works. Its conclusion therefore depends on interpreting the screen capture as a solicitation, not on demonstrated delivery or a spoken guarantee.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough reading leaves out the video's own invitation: its title promises free gift cards and codes, and its description tells viewers to click the pinned-comment link. The footage then presents purported code generation and directs users toward sponsor offers to unlock content. An unintelligible transcript does not turn those promotional elements into a critical demonstration.

opening.argument: The visible Walmart promotion has recognizable offer mechanics: it specifies 100 points, identifies a $250 gift-card reward, and notes purchase requirements. Another screen says sponsor offers must be completed before content is unlocked. That supports an interpretation of a conditional rewards promotion, not a claim that every visitor immediately receives cash or a usable card. The record does not show a deposit to the creator, a promised investment return, or a recruited downline, and it does not verify either fulfillment or nonfulfillment. The appropriate distinction is between an offer's advertised conditions and proof that the offer is fraudulent.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The address and birth-date screens are concerning, but the opening does not show where submitted data goes or how it is used. Likewise, an offer gate establishes a condition for access, not that the promised reward is impossible. The visible purchase-requirement notice matters when assessing whether this is a conditional promotion.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Disclosed purchase requirements do not resolve the mismatch between the free-card pitch and the filmed path. The title advertises free branded codes; the generator presents a purported search for unused codes; and access is then locked behind sponsor offers. The separate Walmart flow requests an address and date of birth. No deposit or downline is necessary for those facts to support the concern here, and the record does not establish that the advertised codes work.
